newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Ousted Cambodian prince replaced as premier.
newsitem.headline: Ousted Cambodian prince replaced as premier.

text.p: Cambodia's ousted Prince Norodom Ranariddh on Wednesday was replaced as first prime minister by Foreign Minister Ung Huot in a move that drew immediate fire from Cambodia's exiled opposition.

Second Prime Minster Hun Sen, who ousted Ranariddh early last month, said the National Assembly's overwhelming approval of Ung Huot signalled the end of Cambodia's turmoil and proved he did not seize power.

"The crisis is now over," Hun Sen told reporters after 86 members of the 120-seat parliament voted by secret ballot in favour of Ung Huot's nomination as first prime minister. A total of 99 assembly members attended the Wednesday session.
"I did not seize power," Hun Sen said, referring to two days of battles in Phnom Penh and his unilateral ousting of Ranariddh on July 6.
"If I seized power I would not have supported the vote to choose a new first prime minister," he said.
Hun Sen said he and Ung Huot were preparing to visit King Norodom Sihanouk in Beijing where the king is receiving medical treatment.

Sihanouk said late last month he would not recognise Ung Huot as first premier as the post belonged to his son, Ranariddh. The king also said that a vote on a new first prime minister by an incomplete parliament would be invalid.
The United States and the Association of South East Asian Nations both said soon after the prince's ouster that they still recognised the prince as first prime minister.
Ung Huot told parliament he was honoured to have been elected first prime minister and said the main task of the government was to strengthen political, economic and social institutions.
"I am determined to try by all means to make the Kingdom of Cambodia a genuine state governed by the rule of law with strong political, legal, economic and social institutions," he told the assembly.
"The government economic and financial policies over the next few years will be geared towards consolidating marcoeconomic stability and laying a solid foundation for sustained development," he said.
He also promised to work closely with Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP) in preparing for elections scheduled for May, and said he would stand down as first prime minister at that time.

Many royalist supporters fled the country in the wake of Hun Sen's takeover and a subsequent crackdown on the royalist FUNCINPEC party, including some 20 members of parliament from Ranariddh's party and a smaller allied party.
Members of the Cambodian opposition in Bangkok said Ung Huot's nomination was illegal.

"The appointment today by the National Assembly in an atmosphere of intimidation and fear, of Mr Ung Huot is totally illegal," the Union of Cambodian Democrats opposition group said in a statement released in the Thai capital.

Ung Huot was nominated by FUNCINPEC members who stayed in the country. Hun Sen backed the nomination, saying he wanted to keep the CPP coalition with FUNCINPEC in place and that FUNCINPEC should select a new first prime minister.

But political analysts said there were articles in the constitution, including the need for the king's approval, making it difficult to push through Ung Huot's selection as premier fully in accordance with the charter,
Earlier on Wednesday, the National Assembly voted to strip Ranariddh of his parliamentary immunity clearing the way for his prosecution for alleged crimes if he returned to Cambodia.

The prince was out of the country at the time of his ouster. Hun Sen said later Ranariddh was free to come back, but that he would have to face charges for his illegal negotiations with the outlawed Khmer Rouge guerrilla group and for alleged weapons smuggling.
The prince has dismissed the accusations and called from abroad for opposition to his former co-premier and coalition partner.
